title: Spot the JSONB concurrent-counter bug
description: Below is a service method that tries to increment metadata.viewCount inside a JSONB column. Click the line that causes the lost-update bug under concurrent requests, and explain the root cause in one sentence (the keyword 'read-modify-write' or 'lost update' is expected).

widgetConfig.errorMessage: Bug report: under load, two concurrent POST /articles/:id/view requests both succeed, yet the final viewCount only goes up by 1 instead of 2. No SQL error, no log entry — just a silent miscount.

modelAnswer: Line 5 is the classic read-modify-write race. Postgres stores JSONB as a single binary blob — to bump one key, the ORM must SELECT the whole metadata, mutate it in JS, then UPDATE the whole column back. Two concurrent requests both read the same value (say 7), both write 8, and one increment is lost. The fix is to move viewCount out of JSONB into a real int column and increment with `UPDATE article SET view_count = view_count + 1 WHERE id = $1` — Postgres takes a row lock and the addition is atomic.

title: Match the advanced-modeling toolbox to its use case
description: Lesson 8 introduces five advanced modeling tools. Match each to the scenario where the lesson recommends it.

pairs.definition: Address fields (street/city/country) live on the Author table as address_* columns — no extra table, no extra join.
Book + Article + Photo all share a 'media' table with a discriminator column — small per-subtype variation.
Subtypes diverge sharply: separate tables per subclass, joined by FK at query time.
An in-memory hydration target built from a raw SQL or QB expression — no DB table backs it.
Auto-generate Article.slug from title before the row is inserted.

modelAnswer: Embeddables flatten value objects into the parent row. STI = one table + discriminator for shape-similar subtypes. TPT = separate tables joined when needed for shape-divergent subtypes. Virtual entities are read-only projections over raw SQL. Lifecycle hooks fire inside the Unit of Work and are the canonical place for derived-field logic like slug generation.

title: Pick the right strategy for an inheritance scenario (decision tree)
description: The librarian wants one catalogue page that shows Books, Magazines, and Newspapers together. Books and Magazines share 80% of fields; Newspapers diverge with a publishDate, no ISBN, and a region. Walk the tree to pick STI, TPT, or mapped superclass.

root.question: First question: do you need polymorphic queries (find all media in one query, irrespective of subtype)?

options.label: Yes, the catalogue lists everything in one page.
No, each subtype has its own page and query path.

outcome.explanation: Mapped superclass is fine here — share fields at the TypeScript level, no inheritance at the DB level. Simplest, no discriminator, no joins. The lesson recommends this whenever you don't actually need polymorphic SQL.

q-shape.question: Polymorphic queries required. How shape-similar are the subtypes?

options.label: Mostly the same — books and magazines share 80% of fields, newspapers diverge a bit.

outcome.explanation: STI (Single Table Inheritance) wins. One 'media' table + a discriminator column. Polymorphic queries are a single SELECT. Newspaper-only columns are NULL on Book/Magazine rows — acceptable when shape overlap is high.

options.label: Strongly different — different required fields, different constraints, different indexes.

outcome.explanation: TPT keeps schemas clean but every polymorphic query becomes a JOIN or UNION across subtype tables. The lesson notes TPT pays its tax on every read — only worth it when the shapes really diverge AND the polymorphic queries are rare.

If the shapes are identical, you don't need inheritance at all — make it one entity with a `kind` field and put behaviour differences in services. Inheritance buys you nothing here and costs maintenance.

modelAnswer: Decision rule: first ask 'do I need polymorphic queries?'. If no, mapped superclass (TS-only). If yes and shapes are similar, STI. If yes and shapes diverge, TPT (and accept the JOIN tax). If shapes are identical, you don't need inheritance — one entity + kind field.
